1:
The sign is a sequel to the one before it, and Charles Ellicott states the difference exactly. The similitude—better called the parable dramatised—is the darker side of the earlier imagery. There the vessel was still on the wheel and capable of being reshaped; now it is baked and hardened, so that no change is possible, and if it is unfit for its purpose there is nothing left but to break it—the fit symbol of an obdurate people whose polity, nationality and religious system had to be broken up. John Calvin adds the point of both visions: the Jews thought themselves exempt from the common lot of men because chosen as a peculiar people; but being covenant-breakers their glorying was vain, since the adoption of Abraham’s race carried a condition, to walk before God and be perfect, and when they all became apostates the covenant as to them was abolished. The vessel is broken so that they might understand that they were earthen vessels, and being admonished of their fragility might no longer be proud as if they possessed a perpetual happiness. Adam Clarke notes that the prophets taught often by symbolic actions, and dates the discourse to the reign of Jehoiakim.

The vessel itself is described with care. Keil and Delitzsch derive its name from a verb meaning to pour out, a jar with a narrow neck named from the sound of liquid poured from it; the potter is named, they observe, to mark it as a jar which on breaking would shiver into many fragments. John Gill derives the name the same way. Ellicott adds that its form is an example of onomatopoeia in the history of language. On the elders, Ellicott says the representatives of the civil and ecclesiastical rulers were to witness this acted prophecy of the destruction of all they held most precious; Clarke identifies the ancients of the priests as chiefs of the twenty-four classes David established. Matthew Henry finds it strange that great men should obey a poor prophet’s summons and follow him out of the city not knowing where or why, and supposes that though most elders were disaffected a few looked on him as a prophet of the Lord. Persons of rank, he adds, honour God by attending the ministry of the word, and should think it no disparagement. He also explains the repetition: the corruption of man makes precept upon precept necessary, since we are unapt to receive and apt to let slip the things of God, so that the irreclaimable may at least be inexcusable.

The gate named next is the standing crux. Ellicott calls the Hebrew obscure: the received version adopts a doubtful etymology connecting the word with the sun, and so with the east; the Latin version and most modern scholars render it the gate of pottery; the Greek treats it as a proper name. Since no such gate appears in the topographical lists and the two gates leading into the valley were the Fountain and the Dung gates, it has been inferred that this was a small postern opening where the valley was filled with rubbish—on which supposition the name of the gate and its use may have determined the command. Calvin declines to settle it, inclining to the solar sense and supposing the gate so called because it looked toward the rising sun, while noting that the valley lay south rather than east. He records renderings of it as the potsherd gate, before which the broken vessels and the filth from the temple lay, as the gate of the dunghill, and as the gate of the burnings, from the practice of burning children in the valley opposite—all of which would designate the south gate. Gill and Ellicott explain why the valley was chosen: it had been the scene of the most hateful idolatry, and Jerusalem was to be made like it for pollution and bloodshed.
3:
The address begins with the kings, and the plural is variously explained. John Gill offers three possibilities—the king and his queen, the king and his sons, or the king with his nobles—since only one king reigned at a time, and takes him to be Zedekiah. Charles Ellicott makes the plural include the reigning king and his heir, and names Jehoiakim instead. John Calvin is less interested in who they were than in their being addressed at all. The prophet did not spare even kings, as God had commanded him to act boldly and show no respect of persons, and addressed them first because those who had sinned most grievously rightly bore the first reproof. Heavenly truth ought to subdue everything high in the world; kings bear such treatment very ill, wishing to be free from every yoke, but if they do not now acknowledge their subjection to God’s word they must at last come before his tribunal. Teachers, he adds, ought to reprove small and great alike after this example. Ellicott finds the next phrase deliberately chosen: the tingling ears occur in the prophecy of doom on the earlier sanctuary, and seem meant to recall the fate that fell on Shiloh, the ruin of the first sanctuary being the type of the second.

The reasons for the sentence follow, the first being the most general. Adam Clarke and John Wesley read the estranging of the place as devoting it to a purpose quite contrary to that for which it was given; Ellicott glosses it as alienating it from its true Lord, and refers the guilt specially to Manasseh. Calvin uses the first charge to answer an objection. None of these would willingly have confessed the accusation; they would have said they had not forsaken God, being the children of Abraham, but only wished to add to his worship, and asked why it should be a reproach that they worshipped here as well as in the temple and did not even spare their own children. God shows by a single expression that these are frivolous evasions, since he is not acknowledged except where what he orders is obediently received; he is forsaken as soon as men turn aside from his pure word. Calvin observes that God had consecrated the whole of Judea to himself—not that sacrifices were to be offered everywhere, but that while the Jews worshipped as taught the whole land was as it were an altar and a temple.

The second charge is the blood, and here they divide. Ellicott notes that the words seem at first to refer to the sacrifices which had made the valley infamous, but since those are mentioned separately in the next verse he thinks the prophet meant the innocent blood with which Manasseh had filled Jerusalem, the same word being used elsewhere. Calvin keeps the two together and uses the second to amplify the first: the people had not only despised God and his law but cruelly destroyed their innocent infants, so that they stand guilty not only of impiety but of a brutal savagery in not sparing innocent blood. On the god named, Ellicott identifies him with the deity of those sacrifices and observes that the terms of the guilt and its punishment are all but identical with an earlier passage. Clarke takes the name as a general title for all the popular idols, and Wesley the same, noting that the two names signify the same thing, one meaning a lord and the other a king. Keil and Delitzsch set out the structure rather than the substance: the punishment is given at large in two series which explain the emblematic act with the pitcher, the first introduced by the word that intimates its meaning and the second bound up with its breaking. Gill reads the high places as the temples where the image stood and the altars where sacrifice was made.
6:
The renaming of the place is the first stroke of the sentence, and the name itself is contested. John Calvin reviews the derivations and settles none. Some take the word simply for hell or eternal death, which he will not admit; more probable, he thinks, is the derivation from a word meaning a drum, on the supposition that drums were beaten when the infants were killed so that their cries might not be heard; but as that is only conjecture he reports another, from a verb meaning to be decorous or beautiful, an etymology with something apparently in its favour. Charles Ellicott refers the reader to his earlier note without repeating it, and John Gill attends instead to the formula that introduces the threat, observing that the days coming are close at hand and that the word of attention prefixed both calls for wonder and assures the certain performance of what follows. Calvin explains why the threat seemed incredible: the Jews had chosen that very place for their superstitions and thought a great part of their safety depended on that worship, so that to hear it renamed the valley of slaughter overturned what they most relied on. He singles out the clause saying that such a thing never came into God’s mind. That one expression, he says, fulminates against all the inventions with which men delight themselves: where there is no command, whatever is attempted is frivolous and useless.

The making void of counsel is the point at which the sign and the sentence meet. Ellicott shows how. The Hebrew verb is onomatopoetic, representing the gurgling of water flowing from the mouth of a jar, and contains the root of the word rendered bottle; it was chosen with an allusive reference to it, such play on sound and sense being quite in accordance with the genius of Hebrew prophecy though usually impossible to reproduce in another language. Its primary meaning is to pour out or spill, and so to waste or bring to nought. He adds that some interpreters have supposed the words were accompanied by corresponding acts, and that the bottle, which the prophet had brought filled with water, was now emptied in the sight of the people. Gill notices the same wordplay, that their schemes were made to appear as empty as the earthen bottle in his hand, and that there is an elegant paronomasia between the verb and the noun.

What that counsel was is read two ways. Adam Clarke supposes it refers to some determination to proclaim themselves independent and pay no more tribute to the Chaldeans. Calvin takes it religiously, as the whole scheme by which they thought to secure themselves. They had persuaded themselves that it was abundantly sufficient to reconcile them to God that they spared not their own children and performed their worship so zealously; hypocrites are commonly inflated with this presumption, preferring what pleases them to what pleases God and adoring their own inventions. The plain meaning of the threat, he says, is that God will frustrate all their plots and projects and make them as vain and empty as the bottle. He then makes a concession about the word counsel. There is neither wisdom nor counsel in deluded men while they devise new and frivolous modes of worship; but the Apostle observes that all the fictions men devise have in them some appearance of wisdom, and wherever our imagination carries us we think ourselves wise, while whatever God prescribes becomes insipid to us. The prophet therefore concedes the name of counsel to vain inventions, though improperly, since experience teaches how much delight men take in their superstitions, wishing to subject God to their own will. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense, that God will make void all the counsels the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem had taken to escape his righteous judgments.
8:
The city’s fate is stated in two words, and the commentators take them differently. John Gill reads the hissing as directed at the city by its enemies and occasioned by its desolation, when its walls should be broken down, its houses burnt and its inhabitants put to the sword or carried captive. Charles Ellicott attends to the last clause instead, observing that the word rendered plagues is used in its wider and yet stricter sense to include all the blows or smitings that are thought of as coming from the hand of God. John Calvin takes both words as one problem in translation. The Hebrew term signifies both desolation and astonishment, since in that language the same word often expresses cause and effect together, desolation being the cause and astonishment the effect; the versions divide accordingly, some giving one and some the other, and the literal rendering is that God will set this city for an astonishment and for a hissing. The hissing itself he calls a mark of detestation rather than of scorn, and notes that the desolation of the whole land and the ruin of the holy city where God had chosen a habitation might justly have filled all who saw it with terror. He also explains why the denunciation is enlarged rather than stated once. Had the prophet used only a single sentence or a common mode of speaking in describing the ruin, they would not have been moved at all, so he advances with greater vehemence in order to penetrate hard and perverse hearts; and he always speaks in the person of God, that the denunciation might have greater weight. It was not enough, Calvin adds, that a calamity should be announced without adding that it came from God’s own hand and was the just punishment of their wickedness.

The next verse is the extremity of the sentence, and it is handled soberly. Gill notes that the famine should be so pressing as to bring this about, and that the prophet who foretold it was a witness of it and left it on record. Ellicott hears in the words an echo, almost a quotation, from the curses of Deuteronomy, whose woes had furnished the prophet with both imagery and language, and points to the Lamentations as proof of the fulfilment. He then draws the retribution out: by that dread law the people were to pay the penalty of their sin in the sacrifices where, offending at once against natural affection and against the faith of their fathers, they had slain their own sons and daughters. Adam Clarke refers the words to the later siege of the city under the Romans, and thinks the prophet may have had that in view as well. Calvin makes the same historical point from the historian who describes that siege at large, and adds the reasoning behind the horror. Extreme despondency has sometimes driven men to kill their wives and children, or to build a pyre in the forum and die with them, but for a father to eat the flesh of his son is more barbarous still; the prophet is therefore describing an unusual vengeance which cannot be classed with the calamities that usually happen to mankind. He does not hesitate to justify it: those who had in so many ways and for so long provoked God exceeded the crimes of all nations in impiety and ingratitude, so that the punishment was just, though it cannot be mentioned without horror. The whole, he insists, is to be ascribed to God’s judgment, since the Hebrew makes him the agent—I will cause them to eat—and those who had sacrificed their children to idols were judicially brought to these straits.
10:
The breaking is the point of the errand, and they explain both why it is done and what it says. John Calvin reconstructs the sequence: the prophet was sent to the potter’s house for the bottle, then went to the valley and spoke against their corrupt worship, and at last broke the bottle before his witnesses. The sign was necessary for a people not only ignorant but perverse and obstinate; it taught the doom of the city and sealed the prophecy, the vessel being broken so that a visible act might show the near approach of a vengeance they had no apprehension of. He adds a caution: signs are useless when the word of God does not shine forth, as superstitious men practise ceremonies which are only histrionic acts, and God never commanded a prophet to show a sign without adding doctrine—which is why the breaking is followed by a repetition of the message. Matthew Henry gives the same reason from the other side, that what they see will affect them more than what they only hear, which is the intention of sacramental signs. John Gill draws three points from the likeness: nothing is more easily broken than an earthen vessel, and so easily was Jerusalem destroyed; an earthen pot can resist no force, as the inhabitants could not withstand the besieging army; and a broken vessel must be replaced rather than mended, as city and temple were rebuilt and not repaired.

The relation of this sign to the earlier one is where they are most interesting. Henry imagines the objection and answers it. The people had been compared to the potter’s clay, easily marred in the making, and might say that this was past with them, being hardened long since; and what though they were, he replies, for the vessel is as soon broken in any man’s hand as the clay is marred in the potter’s, and its case is worse, since clay though marred may be moulded again, while a hardened vessel once broken can never be pieced. Charles Ellicott makes the same contrast and qualifies it. Those who watched knew the imagery, since an older psalm had portrayed the anointed king breaking the nations in pieces like a potter’s vessel; but it was new and strange to hear the words applied to themselves, and to see their own nation treated not as clay that could be remodelled but as a vessel which once broken could never be restored. Happily for Israel, there was a depth of divine compassion which the parable failed to represent: as far as that generation went the punishment was final, yet there was hope for the nation, and the fragments might be gathered from the rubbish where the prophet flung them and brought into a new shape, for uses less glorious than the first but far other than a vessel of dishonour.

Calvin makes the opposite point from the same fact. The calamity was wholly irremediable—the most grievously afflicted sometimes retain some strength and are at length restored, but not here; and it is no objection that God afterwards restored the people, since that was nothing to the ungodly men of that age, the curse remaining on the heads of those who continued obstinate. He notes that the city is named because they thought they had an impregnable fortress in it on account of the temple, and that having profaned the temple and polluted the city they were reminded that no confidence was to be placed there. Adam Clarke refers the unrepairable breaking forward in time, to the destruction under the Romans rather than the Chaldean one, since Jerusalem was healed after seventy years but has not been made whole in the centuries since the later capture. Gill notes only that the Lord of hosts is named as God of armies above and below, able to execute what he threatens.
12:
The comparison is now turned round: the city is to become what the valley already was. John Calvin states the reversal plainly—as the valley shall be the place of slaughter and take its name from that, so shall Jerusalem be—and notes an ellipsis in the clause of the kind common in Hebrew, the full sentence running that God will so deal with the place as to make this city like the valley. Adam Clarke and John Wesley gloss the name in the same terms, a place of slaughter and destruction, Wesley adding burials. Charles Ellicott finds the reference doubly allusive, partly to the state of the valley as a heap of ruins and rubbish, partly to the meaning of the name itself as a place spat upon and scorned. John Gill makes the parallel exact, that what was done to the earthen bottle shall be done to the city and its inhabitants. Calvin adds a note on the effect of the preaching: they were kindled into rage on hearing it, as the next chapter shows, yet God purposed, however irreclaimable they were, to let them know what was approaching; and though they did not believe the prophet, God touched and even deeply wounded their consciences, so that they were miserable before the event came.

The particulars that follow are given, Calvin says, because the general threat was hard to believe. Jerusalem was a wide city and splendidly built, with many large and elegant houses and the royal palaces, and he enumerates them to show that none of this would prevent God from demolishing the whole. This deserves particular notice, he adds, because Satan dazzles our eyes whenever he suggests anything that gives a hope of defence, while what God threatens we think vain and as it were fabulous; and since so gross a hypocrisy prevailed, the prophet rightly tried to shake off whatever might deceive them. No house shall be exempt from slaughter and no palace shall protect its inhabitants; they shall be defiled on account of the dead bodies found everywhere, which Scripture often names as a pollution. He weighs a preposition in the last clause, which some read as causal—on account of all the houses—but takes rather as explanatory, so that the prophet is speaking of all the houses on which they burned incense. Gill glosses the houses of Jerusalem as those where the common people dwelt.

The roofs are explained by Ellicott from the architecture. The flat roofs of eastern houses were used for exercise and also, as in the apostle’s vision at Joppa, for prayer and meditation, and seem to have been specially chosen, as was natural, for worship addressed to the host of heaven; the two altars on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz were probably so situated. Where men had been accustomed to keep the holy days of the Feast of Tabernacles they had celebrated their idolatrous rites instead. He supports the practice from an ancient geographer who describes a people of the desert worshipping the sun and offering incense on an altar on the roofs of their houses. On the construction of the clause about defilement he notes a difficulty affecting the construction but not the sense, and prefers the rendering that makes the phrase describe the place as the defiled one rather than describing the houses as defiled like it.
14:
The chapter ends with the message repeated in a second place, and everyone notices the repetition. John Calvin explains why it was needed. The prophet had been led to the very place when he foretold the punishment, so that his doctrine might be more efficacious, God intending that he preach in the valley then notorious for false worship; now he goes to the temple and delivers the same message. From this we learn how great the stupidity of the people must have been, since the repetition was not unnecessary: knowing them tardy and slow, God had them warned twice and in two different places. He notes that the court is named because the people were not allowed into the temple itself but assembled there. The prophet had to speak not to a few or in a corner but to the whole people, and to make them witnesses of his prophecy; and there is nothing new in what he says, since he was bidden to declare the same calamity twice, the Jews being so hardened that they could not easily be moved. That other cities are joined with Jerusalem, Calvin adds, is no wonder, since he thereby intimates that the whole land was guilty.

Charles Ellicott makes the same contrast a matter of audience: the acted sermon had been preached in the valley before a few chosen representatives of priests and people, and is followed by one addressed to the whole assembled congregation announcing the same doom. John Wesley agrees, noting that the court was common to all the people, where the most might hear, and that the prophet came back by God’s direction having discharged the errand on which he was sent. Adam Clarke supposes he had gone to the valley and there repeated the discourse he had delivered a little before to the chief priests and elders. Ellicott adds a judgement about the report itself: the address could hardly have been confined to a single verse, so that we probably have only the summary of a discourse so like what had gone before that the prophet did not think it necessary to report it at length. John Gill marks the moment simply, that the prophet came from the valley when he had broken the bottle and delivered his prophecy before the elders and the priests.

The reason given for the sentence is hardness, and Calvin takes the last verse as the chapter’s conclusion in more than a formal sense. It confirms, he says, what has been observed throughout, that they had fallen not through ignorance but through perverseness: they had learned clearly enough from the law what was right and had often been warned by the prophets, so that their wickedness and untameable spirit appeared in rejecting what they had heard. The passage teaches that no pardon is left for those who avowedly reject the yoke of God; and this ought to be noticed, since we see how difficult it is to subdue men even when they confess that what they hear is the word of God. There is in all mankind an innate perverseness, so that hardly one in a hundred allows himself to be ruled by that word, and those who harden the neck are unworthy of mercy. Though hardness is in all mortals, he adds, a greater impiety and pride show themselves when the doctrine of salvation is made known and not received, for then men hear God speaking and yet rob him of his authority; and it follows that the more clearly God makes known his truth, the less ground of excuse there is. Clarke explains the figure from husbandry, a metaphor taken from unruly and unbroken oxen which resist the yoke and break and run away with their gears, so that this people had broken and destroyed the yoke of the law.
